correctedCritiques.con-selective-hostile-source-survival: Strongest feature: The reply distinguishes textual authenticity from representative survival, arguing that an untampered hostile document may still be nonrepresentative if Christian copyists preferentially preserved testimony useful to Christian claims. Principal limitation: The excerpt supplies neither manuscripts, comparative survival patterns, preservation history, nor evidence that useful hostile writings endured more often than unfavorable or irrelevant pagan material. Live burden: The skeptic must show that this selection mechanism is historically probable enough to weaken the independence of witnesses without converting every archival absence into evidence of Christian filtering. Locked score: The strong band recognizes conceptual sophistication, direct engagement with representativeness, and carefully qualified possibility, while withholding greater credit because the mechanism, scope, and documentary basis remain materially underdeveloped.
correctedCritiques.pro-limited-spread-does-not-defeat-ident: Strongest feature: The reply narrows the claim by arguing that early bishops, priests, and deacons, persisting amid conflict through Nicaea, can identify a structured community without requiring Christianity to have been prevalent. Principal limitation: Institutional persistence neither answers selective preservation nor establishes independence from Christian informants, and it cannot uniquely identify Catholic continuity rather than one community among several competing Christian lineages. Live burden: The affirmative must define the Catholic markers, show how outside testimony was acquired, and explain why continuity of offices supports exclusive apostolic and resurrection claims. Locked score: The mixed band rewards clear scope control, institutional evidence, and acknowledgment of disorder, but reflects overconfident identification and failure to answer representativeness, transmission, and plural-continuity objections.
